title: After the Door Opens
subtitle: The Lanternweald — fifth expansion pass
content:
The last chapter of the archive report began with a blank line.

Neri had left it there deliberately, a space where the erased signature from the Closed Bells ledger might one day be identified through evidence or voluntary testimony. The committee had finally accepted that not knowing was different from refusing to care.

Severus stood beside the display case as the first visitors entered.

He had volunteered an hour of cataloging guidance each week, not because anyone had demanded it, but because he wanted the archive to become a place where students could learn how not to turn uncertainty into fiction.

Orin was the first to arrive.

"I have a question," they said.

Severus sighed.

"An auspicious beginning."

Orin smiled and opened their notebook.

They had revised the wartime biography once more, replacing grand claims with citations, conflicting testimony, and a section about people whose accounts remained incomplete. They didn't ask Severus to approve every sentence. They asked whether the evidence had been represented fairly.

He read the opening.

Then he nodded.

"Better."

Orin looked as though they might faint from happiness.

I took the tea tray to the small table by the window, where Neri had laid out the public maintenance records. The door to the private correspondence room remained closed. The emergency structural records were available through the new sign-out system, and the rules were posted at a height visitors could actually read.

It wasn't glamorous.

It was working.

"Tea?" I asked Severus.

He took a cup and sniffed it.

"What have you done?"

"I made tea."

"That much is apparent."

"Is it terrible?"

"It is an ambitious assault on the leaves."

I laughed.

He drank it anyway.

Outside, the first light of morning moved across the stone arches. People were gathering for the reopening of the safe canal path, though the lower service passage remained sealed pending more inspection. The square smelled of fresh bread and damp leaves.

Iroh passed the window carrying a small kettle. Greg was helping set up chairs. Danse spoke with Toph beside the bridge plan, both of them apparently capable of disagreeing without threatening each other's competence. Maui was carrying a crate of lantern hooks with an expression of remarkable restraint.

Six different lives, overlapping without collapsing into one.

Severus watched them through the glass.

"You have a busy day," he said.

"I do."

"Are you coming back for dinner?"

"Yes. If the inspection runs long, I'll send word before the time we agreed."

He nodded.

The simplicity of it still mattered.

We had talked about ethical non-monogamy and my preference for polyamory before the first fragile steps of romance. We'd revisited the agreements when schedules changed, when privacy felt like hiding, and when either of us feared being forgotten. There was no final answer that could make those conversations unnecessary forever.

There was only the decision to keep having them with care.

Severus set down the cup.

"Would you like to see the new catalog heading?" he asked.

"Of course."

He showed me a card labeled PRIVATE MATERIAL — CONSENT REQUIRED.

Underneath, in smaller handwriting, he'd added: HISTORICAL INTEREST DOES NOT CANCEL OWNERSHIP.

I looked at him.

"That's good."

"I am capable of useful work."

"I've noticed."

He leaned closer.

"Your punctuation, however—"

"Severus."

"—remains a danger to public safety."

I laughed.

He smiled.

The afternoon passed with visitors asking questions. Some were angry about the blank line. Some wanted a villain's name, a simple answer, or a story that made the valley's past easier to admire. Orin explained why the evidence did not yet support one.

Severus listened.

He didn't take over when the apprentice hesitated.

That might have been the most important lesson he'd learned to teach.

Near the end of the visit, an older man arrived with a weather-stained ledger leaf wrapped in cloth.

"My mother kept this," he told Orin. "It says a gate was repaired two days before the flood. Does that prove the keeper knew what would happen?"

Orin's hand hovered over the cloth.

Severus was listening from the other side of the room. I saw him take a breath and stop himself from answering first.

"We can look at the date," Orin said, "but not at the paper without your permission. Is this an item you'd like to donate, or are you asking for help understanding it?"

"Just help."

"Then you can keep it."

They placed a clean support on the table so the fragile page could rest without being pressed flat. The ink was faded, but the entry remained legible: one hinge replaced, one length of rope purchased, one signature abbreviated.

Orin compared it with a copy of the public repair ledger.

"This shows maintenance happened," they said. "It doesn't establish what someone knew about the later flood. We would need the weather reports, the instructions issued at the time, and enough context to interpret the abbreviation."

The man looked disappointed.

"I thought it would be the answer."

"So did I," Orin admitted. "When you brought it in."

Severus stepped forward at last.

"That is why we are learning to stop before the conclusion," he said.

Orin looked relieved but not rescued. They asked the visitor whether a non-identifying transcription could be added to the public evidence list. The man agreed to a copy, declined to donate the original, and asked for a receipt confirming the arrangement.

We gave him one.

After he left, I found Severus standing before the now-empty support.

"That was difficult for you," I said.

"What was?"

"Letting Orin work through the question."

He gave me a dry look.

"I found seven imprecisions and two potentially catastrophic assumptions."

"How many did you correct?"

"One, when invited."

I smiled.

He looked toward the corridor where the apprentice was filing the transcription.

"They will make mistakes," he said.

"Yes."

"And they'll have to repair them."

"Also yes."

He studied me.

"You are distressingly content with imperfect people."

"Only when they let me be one too."

For a moment his expression softened in a way I might once have missed.

He reached for my hand. I let him take it.

At closing time, Neri locked the display cases and left the public light on beside the reading shelf. Anyone with a permitted request could return during the next posted hours. A visitor who had been waiting by the archive desk asked whether they could add a name to the Closed Bells record. They had found it in a family notebook, written beside a date and a sketch of the old square.

Neri accepted a copy of the page but did not copy the name into the public ledger.

“Doesn't that solve it?” the visitor asked.

“It gives us another lead,” Neri said. “We have to establish whom the name belonged to, and whether the person consented to being identified.”

Severus turned toward the display. I saw him prepare the kind of correction that could cut a person's enthusiasm in half. Instead he asked for the ink dates, the notebook's known ownership, and the chain of custody. The questions were dry, irritating and necessary.

The visitor looked disappointed. “You don't think my grandmother remembered correctly?”

“I think she may have,” Severus said. “I refuse to make your grandmother's memory less trustworthy by claiming it proves more than it does.”

Orin took notes while Neri arranged a private review appointment. No one promised a revelation. They did preserve the clue.

When the visitor left, I helped Orin put the copying tools away. One of the drawer labels had fallen off, and the smallest ink bottle had leaked onto the cloth. We cleaned it, wrote a new label and put the damaged fabric aside for proper disposal.

“Quite the dramatic finale,” I said.

Severus eyed the stain. “If you require fireworks, I can recommend several imprudent former pupils.”

I laughed, then noticed how tired he looked. He had offered an hour and stayed forty minutes longer.

“Your next volunteer shift is next week,” I said. “Not tonight.”

“I am aware.”

“Then come home.”

He folded his coat over one arm and asked Orin whether any work remained that could not wait. Orin checked the ledger, found none, and sent him away.

The unknown name stayed unknown. The people who might help identify it had a scheduled path into the archive. It was not a triumphant ending, but it was a fairer one than forcing a story to end on command.


The archive would not be held open by one exhausted person's endless willingness to help.

Severus collected his coat.

"Ready?" he asked.

I nodded.

We walked through the Moonroot Door into Spinner's End. The kitchen was warm, and the table held two bowls, clean cups, and a loaf of bread that hadn't yet been subjected to either of our cooking.

He had remembered.

I set down the keys and took off my coat.

"How did the hour go?" I asked.

"Orin was tiresome."

"Did you enjoy it?"

"Immensely."

I smiled.

He reached for my hand.

"May I kiss you?"

"Yes."

The kiss was tender and familiar, no longer a promise that he would become someone else, but a choice to meet me as he was. He held me close for a moment, then let me step back to stir the soup.

We ate while the rain began again outside.

Later, he read by the fire and I wrote in my green notebook. I didn't write a declaration of forever. I wrote what had happened, what we had chosen, and the small ordinary things I wanted to remember.

The door to the archive would open again tomorrow.

So would the door to this house, whenever either of us chose to enter.

I watched Severus turn a page and smile at something only he could see.

Then I returned to my own book, grateful that neither of us needed to be a legend to be loved.
